nodes.title: Identity and access management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.

questions.q: A finance team needs strict isolation of their OCI resources from engineering, but both groups must roll up to the tenancy's overall cost dashboard. Which OCI construct best fits?
choices: Separate OCI tenancies for finance and engineering
Separate VCNs with no peering between them
Separate compartments under the same tenancy
Separate availability domains for each team
questions.explanation: Compartments are logical containers used to organise, isolate, and control access to resources within a single tenancy; policies on compartments enforce isolation while billing still aggregates at the tenancy level. Separate tenancies would split billing entirely, VCNs only isolate networking (not other resources), and ADs are physical infrastructure rather than an organisational boundary.

questions.q: Which statement is valid OCI IAM policy syntax to let members of the group NetAdmins manage Virtual Cloud Networks in the compartment Network?
choices: allow user NetAdmins to manage virtual-network-family in compartment Network
grant group NetAdmins all on virtual-network-family in compartment Network
permit group NetAdmins manage vcn in compartment Network
allow group NetAdmins to manage virtual-network-family in compartment Network
questions.explanation: OCI policy syntax is: Allow <subject> to <verb> <resource-type> in <location> [where <conditions>]. The subject is normally a group or dynamic group, the verb is inspect/read/use/manage, and virtual-network-family is the aggregate resource type covering VCNs, subnets, gateways, and route tables. Allowing 'user' directly is rare, and 'permit'/'grant' are not valid OCI keywords.

questions.q: A script running ON an OCI compute instance must call OCI APIs to manage Object Storage — without any API keys or credentials stored on the instance. What enables this?
choices: A dynamic group matching the instance, with a policy granting the group access — the instance authenticates via instance principals
A free-tier service user account whose API signing key pair is baked into the instance's custom golden image at build time, then rotated quarterly
The instance's public IP address registered as a trusted source in the tenancy's authentication settings
Auth tokens generated for the administrator and written into the instance's cloud-init metadata
questions.explanation: Instance principals let a compute instance authenticate as itself: a dynamic group defines which instances qualify (by compartment, OCID or tags) and IAM policies grant that group permissions — no stored secrets anywhere. Baked-in API keys and tokens in metadata are exactly the stored credentials to avoid, and OCI does not authenticate API callers by source IP.

questions.q: What is the relationship between a tenancy and compartments in OCI?
choices: A tenancy is created inside each compartment to hold that compartment's billing records
The tenancy is the root compartment; all other compartments are created within it as a hierarchy
Tenancies and compartments are unrelated — one organizes users, the other organizes regions
Each subscribed region requires its own separate tenancy, and compartments cannot span more than one of them
questions.explanation: The tenancy IS the root compartment of the account: every other compartment nests beneath it (up to six levels deep), forming the hierarchy used for organization, IAM policy scoping and cost tracking. Compartments are global constructs that span regions, and an account has exactly one tenancy regardless of how many regions it subscribes to.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: You are designing a VCN whose workload must span multiple availability domains for high availability. What is the simplest subnet design?
choices: Create one AD-specific subnet per AD and manually replicate resources
Create regional subnets, which span all availability domains in the region
Create one subnet per fault domain across the region
Use a single AD-specific subnet and rely on cross-region replication
questions.explanation: Regional subnets stretch across every AD in a region, so the same CIDR can host resources in any AD and multi-AD HA designs need only one subnet per tier. AD-specific subnets are a legacy option that force multiple subnets and more IP planning, fault domains do not have their own subnets, and cross-region replication addresses disaster recovery rather than in-region HA.

questions.q: An OCI compute instance in a private subnet must pull packages from Oracle YUM repositories on the Oracle Services Network without sending the traffic over the public internet. Which gateway provides this?
choices: Internet Gateway
NAT Gateway
Service Gateway
Dynamic Routing Gateway (DRG)
questions.explanation: A Service Gateway lets VCN resources reach supported Oracle Services Network endpoints (such as Object Storage and Oracle YUM mirrors) over the Oracle backbone, never traversing the public internet. An Internet Gateway provides bidirectional public-internet access, a NAT Gateway provides egress-only public-internet access, and a DRG connects a VCN to on-premises networks or other VCNs.

questions.q: Instances in a private OCI subnet must download OS updates from repositories on the public internet, but must never accept inbound connections initiated from the internet. Which gateway does this require?
choices: Internet gateway, with security lists blocking inbound traffic to the subnet
Dynamic routing gateway attached to the VCN and advertised over BGP
NAT gateway
Local peering gateway connecting the private subnet to a public VCN
questions.explanation: A NAT gateway gives private-subnet instances outbound-only internet access: connections can be initiated outward, but no inbound connection can be initiated from the internet. An internet gateway enables bidirectional public connectivity (and belongs with public subnets); a DRG connects to on-premises networks; local peering joins VCNs, not the internet.

questions.q: An architect wants firewall rules that apply only to a specific group of compute instances' VNICs, rather than to every resource in the subnet. Which OCI feature provides this?
choices: Security lists referenced from the subnet's route table entries
Network security groups (NSGs) with the rules applied to member VNICs
A WAF policy attached to each instance's primary private IP address
Compartment policies restricting which users may create the instances
questions.explanation: NSGs are virtual firewalls scoped to the VNICs you place in them, so different instance groups in the same subnet can carry different rules. Security lists apply to every VNIC in the subnet (and have nothing to do with route tables); WAF protects HTTP applications at the edge; IAM compartment policies govern who can manage resources, not packet flow.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: While sizing compute instances in OCI, an architect is deciding between flexible and fixed shapes and reviews how they differ. Which statement BEST describes the difference between flexible and fixed compute shapes in OCI?
choices: Flexible shapes let you independently choose OCPU count and memory; fixed shapes use predetermined values
Flexible shapes can be resized while the instance is running; fixed shapes always require a stop and start
Flexible shapes are only available on Ampere ARM processors; fixed shapes are only AMD and Intel
Flexible shapes are billed monthly; fixed shapes are billed per second
questions.explanation: Flexible shapes such as VM.Standard.E4.Flex and VM.Standard.A1.Flex let you pick the exact number of OCPUs and the amount of memory when you provision the instance. Fixed shapes such as VM.Standard2.4 come with a preset CPU and memory configuration. Resizing both types still typically requires a stop, both shape families exist on AMD, Intel, and Ampere, and OCI uses the same per-second billing model for either.

questions.q: A web tier on OCI must automatically add instances when average CPU exceeds 75% and remove them when load subsides. Which combination implements this?
choices: A flexible shape on one instance, since OCPUs are added automatically under load
Two identical instances placed in different fault domains behind a public load balancer with sticky sessions
An instance pool from an instance configuration, with an autoscaling policy on CPU utilization
A burstable instance whose baseline is set to half of its maximum OCPU allocation
questions.explanation: Horizontal autoscaling in OCI is built from an instance configuration (the template), an instance pool (the managed set) and an autoscaling policy on a metric such as CPU. Flexible shapes fix their OCPU count at launch — they don't grow under load; two static instances provide HA, not elasticity; burstable instances flex within one VM only.

questions.q: For a workload that needs the highest IOPS per gigabyte on OCI Block Volumes, which elastic performance tier should you select?
choices: Lower Cost
Balanced
Higher Performance
Ultra High Performance
questions.explanation: OCI Block Volume offers four elastic performance tiers. Ultra High Performance (UHP) targets the most demanding workloads and delivers the highest IOPS-per-GB ratio. Higher Performance offers about 75 IOPS/GB, Balanced (the default) about 60 IOPS/GB, and Lower Cost about 10 IOPS/GB and is suited to cold or archival data.

questions.q: Which OCI Object Storage tier is designed for data that is rarely accessed and can tolerate restore delays measured in hours, at the lowest storage cost?
choices: Standard tier
Infrequent Access tier
Archive tier
Auto-Tiering
questions.explanation: The Archive tier delivers the lowest storage cost and is intended for data that is rarely accessed; objects must be restored before download and restoration typically takes hours. Standard is for active data, Infrequent Access lowers cost for occasionally accessed data with no restore delay, and Auto-Tiering automatically moves Standard objects between hot and infrequent access patterns rather than being a cold-storage tier of its own.

questions.q: An architect is designing a highly available deployment on OCI and must place resources correctly across the provider's physical hierarchy. How does OCI's physical hierarchy of regions, availability domains (ADs), and fault domains (FDs) work?
choices: A region equals an AD; fault domains are logical groupings of multiple regions
A region always contains exactly three ADs; each AD contains a single fault domain
A region contains a single AD; fault domains span across ADs for redundancy
A region contains one or more ADs; each AD is divided into three fault domains
questions.explanation: An OCI region contains one or more availability domains (each AD is an isolated data centre). Inside every AD there are three fault domains, which are independent groupings of hardware that act as failure isolation zones within the AD. Some newer regions are single-AD, while many commercial regions have three ADs.

questions.q: A team is choosing between Oracle Autonomous Database and a self-managed OCI Database System and wants to know what they gain that the self-managed option cannot match. Which capability is unique to Oracle Autonomous Database compared with a self-managed OCI Database System?
choices: Automated patching, backups, scaling, and tuning fully managed by Oracle
Support for the SQL language and PL/SQL
Multi-AD high availability via Data Guard
Pay-per-use OCPU-hour billing
questions.explanation: Autonomous Database is a self-driving managed database whose distinguishing feature is automation of patching, backups, scaling, and performance tuning by Oracle. SQL and PL/SQL are supported by both Autonomous and self-managed Database Systems, multi-AD Data Guard configurations are available on both, and pay-per-use billing applies to both as well.

questions.q: A student wants to run a small Autonomous Database and a Compute instance indefinitely on OCI without being billed. Which description of Always Free resources is correct?
choices: They are only usable during the 30-day Free Trial period and disabled afterwards
They are available indefinitely at no cost within published limits, even after the trial ends
They require a paid subscription but include 300 US dollars in monthly credits
They are only available in OCI Government Cloud regions
questions.explanation: OCI's Always Free programme provides resources such as two AMD VM.Standard.E2.1.Micro instances, two Autonomous Databases, 200 GB of Block Volume, and 20 GB of Object Storage that remain free indefinitely within published quotas, even after the 30-day Free Trial expires. The separate Free Trial provides a one-time US$300 credit usable against paid services and lasts 30 days; both make up the OCI Free Tier.

questions.q: Which OCI service should be used to centrally generate, store, and rotate encryption keys and secrets such as database passwords?
choices: OCI Vault
OCI Bastion
OCI Identity Domains
OCI Audit
questions.explanation: OCI Vault is a managed service that creates and manages master encryption keys (optionally HSM-backed) and stores secrets like passwords or API tokens with versioning and rotation. OCI Bastion brokers secure SSH or RDP sessions into private resources, Identity Domains is the IAM identity layer for users and federation, and Audit captures API activity logs for compliance.
